title: R & M Trade Desk
text:
What’s behind the number

4-instrument cross-asset basket, three single-stocks (AAPL, MSFT, WMT) for idiosyncratic short-vol exposure plus GLD for commodity-vol exposure. Selected from a 12-instrument tested universe; selection bias corrected via DSR (N̂=9 implied independent trials).
3-layer halt framework, Layer 1 hard halts on extreme single-day SPX moves, Layer 4 trailing-90-day drawdown gate, Layer 5 vol-regime auto-resume with 60-day time fallback.
Per-trade defined risk, 16-delta short put, 5-pt long-put protection, weekly Monday entries, gap-aware exit fills, VIX-conditional slippage model.
Exogenous-factor inputs, VIX/VIX3M/VVIX/SKEW for regime classification, IRX for risk-free baseline + cash accrual, HYG-LQD spread + rolling SPY-Treasury correlation for stress detection. See Mechanics for the full list.
Honest aggregation, book Sharpe computed from the equal-weighted aggregate equity curve, not from per-instrument Sharpe averaging. Cross-instrument correlation 0.26 (low) drives the diversification benefit.

title: R & M Trade Desk
text:
Pre-commitment-driven methodology
Every parameter, threshold, and acceptance criterion was locked in version-controlled pre-commitment documents before the OOS backtest ran. Methodology amendments after pre-commitment are logged with date and reason. See Pre-commitments.

title: R & M Trade Desk
text:
Live-monitoring framework
The strategy ships with a Hoeffding trader-application bound that quantifies, in real time, the probability the underlying win-rate has shifted away from the pre-committed baseline. Threshold semantics (50% / 25% / 10% probability bound) trigger reduce-size, freeze, and shut-down actions respectively. See Live Monitoring for the full framework and worked example on the headline basket.

title: R & M Trade Desk
section: What was tested but not used
text:
What was tested but not used
The headline is one of five baskets tested. The four others (SPX-only put-credit-spread, ETF-3 cluster, full 6-instrument book, iron condor variants on the 3-instrument cluster) underperformed the v1.5 anchor. They are reported transparently in the Ablations page, the iron condor variant is particularly informative: adding the call wing systematically lost in the 2018-2024 trending-equity regime.

title: Strategy Mechanics
text:
Entry construction

Structure: Defined-risk put credit spread (short put + long put protection). No call wing, the iron-condor variant tested separately and underperformed (see Ablations).
Short put delta target: −0.16 (one-sigma OTM, BS-Greek-defined via OptionMetrics IV when available; BS pricer fallback when IV missing)
Wing widths: 5 strike points (per-instrument strike-grid specified above)
DTE at entry: 30 to 45 calendar days; selected expiry is the chain whose DTE is closest to 35
Entry frequency: weekly Monday open per instrument (skipped if Monday is a holiday; defer to next session)
One structure per name per week: no overlapping spreads in the same instrument

title: Strategy Mechanics
section: What the headline DOES NOT use
text:
What the headline DOES NOT use
For transparency: the iron-condor architecture (call wing in addition to put wing) was tested and underperformed put-only across every instrument tested in OOS 2018-2024. The call wing systematically lost in the trending-equity regime. See Ablations for the iron-condor result table. The headline is put-only because the data demanded it.

title: Limitations and Disclosures
text: This page lists every material limitation of the strategy and the methodology used to test it. Honest disclosure is not optional, the strategy’s claim to be a defensible piece of work depends on the writeup being explicit about what it does NOT promise.

title: Limitations and Disclosures
text:
Headline-result limitations

1. Selection bias on the 4-instrument basket
The headline basket (AAPL + MSFT + WMT + GLD) was selected from a tested universe of 12 instruments, 3 ETFs (SPX, TLT, GLD) and 9 single-stocks (AAPL, MSFT, GOOGL, JNJ, KO, PG, WMT, JPM, PEP). Selection was made post-hoc on the criterion of positive excess Sharpe in OOS halts_only mode. This is selection bias.
Mitigation: Deflated Sharpe Ratio with implied-independent-trials correction. The 12 raw trials have an average pairwise return correlation of 0.261, giving an implied independent-trials count of N̂ = 9 per Eq. 9 of the Bailey & López de Prado framework. The DSR (PSR) of the headline basket is 1.0000, meaning the headline excess Sharpe of +0.359 is statistically significant against the noise floor of 9 independent trials. PBO via CSCV is 0.0402 (well below the pre-committed 0.30 acceptance threshold).
The selection is acknowledged and quantitatively corrected, not hidden.


2. Risk-free rate assumption
All Sharpe ratios reported as “excess” use a 2.33% annualized risk-free rate, which is the realized average of the CBOE 13-week T-bill yield (IRX) over the OOS window 2018-2024. The OOS period included near-zero rates 2018-2021 and 4-5% rates 2022-2024, so the 2.33% average is the appropriate within-sample anchor.
If a future report needs to use a different risk-free rate (e.g., a forward-looking expectation), the Sharpe will shift. The strategy’s annualized return is 2.41%, so the excess Sharpe is sensitive to the rf assumption: a rf of 2.0% would give Sharpe ≈ +0.95; a rf of 3.0% would give Sharpe ≈ -0.95. The strategy is barely-positive on excess basis in this rate regime.


3. OOS sample size
OOS spans 2018-01-01 to 2024-12-31, ≈ 7 years (1,760 trading days). Effective independent observations at the 30-day forward horizon (typical IC holding window) ≈ 84 non-overlapping windows. The volatility-risk-premium literature (Bollerslev/Tauchen/Zhou 2009) used 17 years of S&P data; ours is 7. The same caveat about limited post-1990 sample (per BTZ §3 footnote 23) applies amplified.

title: Limitations and Disclosures
text:
Strategy-level limitations

4. Tail risk is real and bounded but not zero
Put-credit-spread max-loss-per-spread is bounded by wing widths (5 strike points = $500 per spread per contract, before commissions). With realistic per-trade sizing (1% of equity per spread), absolute drawdown in a single day is bounded. But:

Multi-day cascade events (e.g., Volmageddon Feb 2018) can produce simultaneous emergency exits on multiple positions before the halt framework engages.
The 4-instrument basket’s correlation rises during stress events (typical ρ jump from 0.26 to 0.6+ in a crisis).



5. Strategy capacity is limited
OptionMetrics open-interest data shows our chosen 16-delta strikes have median per-strike OI in the hundreds-to-thousands for AAPL/MSFT/WMT and dozens-to-hundreds for GLD. Scaling beyond ~$5–20M of capital (depending on instrument) likely encounters meaningful market-impact friction beyond what our backtest’s bid-ask slippage model captures.
This is a retail / small-fund strategy, not an institutional one.

title: Limitations and Disclosures
text:
Methodological limitations

6. Iron-condor tested-and-rejected, not avoided
The pre-committed methodology specified iron condors (put + call wings). On the spot-corrected engine, iron condor variants underperformed put-only across every instrument tested. The headline is put-only; the iron-condor result is reported in Ablations as a tested extension with negative result. The decision to ship put-only is evidence-driven, but it differs from the original pre-commitment.


7. Daily-frequency RV components in the realized-vol indicators
Per BTZ 2009 §3.2.1: 5-minute intraday squared returns produce stronger predictability for VRP-based forecasting than daily close-to-close RV. We use daily RV in the engine’s vol-multiplier computation. Without intraday data, we cannot match the BTZ-preferred specification.


8. R² inflation per Boudoukh-Richardson-Whitelaw (2008)
In overlapping multi-period predictive regressions, R² inflates roughly proportionally with horizon × overlap, even in the absence of true predictability. Our 30-day forward window with daily observations creates this pattern.
We mitigate by reporting Hodrick (1992) standard errors (src/metrics/hodrick_se.py) as the primary significance measure for any regression we report, rather than naive Newey-West. R² is reported descriptively only.

title: Limitations and Disclosures
text:
Backtest-environment limitations

9. Synthetic-pricing fallback when OptionMetrics IV missing
OptionMetrics has ~7-15% NaN rate on delta and IV per ticker (concentrated at deep-ITM/OTM strikes where Greeks aren’t computed). Our engine falls back to BS-derived deltas using VIX/100 as ATM-IV proxy when needed. This is a known approximation; magnitude is small at our 16-delta strikes (which have populated deltas in the OptionMetrics data) but worth flagging.


10. Friction-model calibration is best-effort
Slippage, commission, and gap-aware-fill parameters are pre-committed but not directly calibrated to specific broker fee schedules. Real-world results will differ in these dimensions. We err conservative (more slippage in higher-VIX buckets, gap-fills at worst execution).


11. American early-exercise risk on dividend-paying single-stocks
Per Merton (1973) Theorem 13, American puts on dividend-paying stocks have positive probability of premature exercise. Our headline basket has 3 of 4 names paying dividends (AAPL, MSFT, WMT, GLD is a commodity ETF and does not pay dividends).
Pricing approximation: we use BS European-style for all wheel names. This undervalues the option for the counterparty (we underestimate the premium they’d rationally demand). Magnitude is small at our 16-delta OTM entry strikes; grows when underlying drops materially and put becomes ITM near ex-dividend dates. We do not model the assignment cash-flow precisely; reported P&L represents OTM-expiration economics.


12. BS pricing biases (the source of VRP itself)
Per Black & Scholes (1973) page 654 empirical test on 545 OTC option contracts: BS systematically overvalues options on high-variance underlyings and undervalues low-variance. This bias is the structural source of the volatility risk premium we harvest. We do not “out-predict” BS; we systematically take the side of the trade where empirical VRP is positive in the historical record. The strategy’s edge is contingent on this bias persisting in future periods.

title: Limitations and Disclosures
text:
Exogenous-factor data limitations

13. TWS-sourced macro factors
The exogenous factors used by the engine (VIX, VIX3M, VVIX, SKEW, IRX, TNX, HYG, LQD, SPY, SPX bars) are sourced from the Interactive Brokers TWS feed snapshot frozen at commit time. These are point-in-time by the snapshot date but lack the explicit “as-of-decision-time” stamping that institutional data providers (Bloomberg, Refinitiv) provide. We use pd.Series.asof(today) to enforce no-look-ahead, but small backfill artifacts in the source feed are possible.


14. Per-ticker underlying spot from OptionMetrics IvyDB Securities
The 4-instrument basket’s underlying daily spots (AAPL, MSFT, WMT, GLD) are sourced from the OptionMetrics IvyDB Securities file (queried via WRDS). This is the same vendor as the option chain data, which ensures secid alignment across the chain and the underlying. Daily close prices match published exchange records on spot-checked reference dates (e.g., AAPL 2018-04-16 = $175.82, matches exchange record).

title: Limitations and Disclosures
text:
Live monitoring limitations

15. Hoeffding bound is worst-case
The bound holds for any bounded RV regardless of distribution, but it is loose. Tighter bounds exist (e.g., Bernstein, normal-approximation) for distributions where assumptions hold. We use Hoeffding for distribution-free guarantees; this means the 50/25/10% thresholds are conservative, the actual probability of regime change is at most these values, not exactly these values.


16. Pre-committed μ does not adapt over time
The committed μ baseline is computed from the OOS backtest and held fixed in live deployment. If we adapted μ live (e.g., updating to the rolling 12-month observed win rate), we would lose the pre-commitment property and the framework would become a moving-goalpost circular reference. Trade-off: occasional false-negatives in genuine regime changes that look “normal” relative to the pre-committed baseline.

title: Limitations and Disclosures
text:
Multi-testing limitations beyond the headline

17. Mode comparison creates a second multiple-testing layer
The ablation includes mode comparisons (naked vs halts_only). Comparing the better of the two modes against the anchor introduces a second selection layer beyond the basket-selection layer corrected via DSR + PBO.
The headline only reports the halts_only mode result. The naked-mode results are reported in the ablation pages for transparency, not as candidates.

title: Pre-commitments
text:
Wheel basket (PRE_COMMITMENT_WHEEL.md)

Basket selection (locked)

Primary 9-name basket: AAPL, MSFT, GOOGL, JNJ, KO, PG, WMT, JPM, PEP
Robustness 7-name strict: drops JPM, PEP
Robustness 8-name: adds JPM only



5-layer wheel architecture

Layer 1 Regime-conditional delta: VIX bottom Q → 0.15, mid → 0.20, top → 0.25
Layer 2 Per-name vol-adjusted strikes: RV>35% widens delta by +0.05
Layer 3 Per-name 30-day RV forecaster: XGBoost on HAR-RV + exogenous, sizing = clip(target_rv/forecast, 0.4, 1.5), skip if forecast > 95th pctile
Layer 4 Earnings-aware management: 7-day blackout pre-earnings, narrow CCs
Layer 5 Fundamental-only defensive rolls: entry premise broken (EPS guidance cut >20%, dividend cut, 2-notch downgrade, sector underperformance + name residual return < −10%)



Disclosed limitations (per §1.1, §2.1)

8 of 9 names pay dividends → American early-exercise risk on ITM puts (Merton Theorem 13). Pricing approximation: BS European-style for all wheel names; magnitude small at OTM entry, grows ITM near ex-dividend dates.
HAR-RV forecaster uses daily-frequency RV components, not 5-minute intraday (per BTZ §3.2.1 caveat).



Acceptance gates

9-name primary Sharpe ≥ 7-name strict − 0.05 (else strict becomes headline)
Each ML/forecaster head meets criterion or falls back
DSR ≥ 0.95
PBO ≤ 0.30
Reproducibility test passes
Within-sector probe (KO/PEP correlation) reported regardless of pass/fail

title: Thesis: Why Variance Risk Premium
text:
Across stock indexes and individual stocks, the implied variance from option prices systematically exceeds the realized variance over matching forward windows. This gap, the variance risk premium, has been documented as strongly negative for the S&P 500, S&P 100, and Dow Jones indexes (large t-statistics on both raw and log forms), smaller-magnitude negative for the Nasdaq 100 and most individual stocks, and statistically distinguishable from zero across multiple decades of data.
The premium is not arbitrageable away because hedging variance risk requires either long-vol options positions (which lose money on average if you collect the premium by selling) or continuous dynamic delta-hedging that incurs friction. Both reset the risk to a different form: short-vol exposure with tail risk, or vega-and-friction exposure to dynamic-hedge slippage.
Investors are willing to pay this premium because variance shocks correlate negatively with index returns, variance risk is “insurance against market drawdowns,” and insurance commands a premium. Classical CAPM beta captures only a small portion of the empirically observed magnitude. Fama-French three-factor models leave large residuals. The premium appears to compensate exposure to a separate volatility-risk factor.

title: Thesis: Why Variance Risk Premium
text:
What our strategy harvests
The strategy systematically sells defined-risk volatility structures (iron condors and cash-secured puts) on instruments where the premium has been documented. We collect the option premium up front, accept the tail-risk exposure (capped by the wing widths on iron condors and by share-assignment mechanics on the wheel), and manage active positions with five exit fates.
Specifically:

5-instrument iron condor cluster (SPX, RUT, NDX, TLT, GLD): captures equity-index VRP plus cross-asset (bond, gold) VRP. The strategy harvests the structurally negative VRP across asset classes; correlation diversification reduces portfolio variance without giving up expected return.
9-name adaptive wheel basket (AAPL, MSFT, GOOGL, JNJ, KO, PG, WMT, JPM, PEP): captures single-name VRP via cash-secured puts and covered calls. Strategy adapts strike delta to the prevailing volatility regime, widens strikes per name when realized vol is elevated, and uses an XGBoost realized-vol forecaster for sizing.

title: Thesis: Why Variance Risk Premium
section: What this strategy does NOT claim
text:
What this strategy does NOT claim

Not statistical arbitrage. The premium is a real risk premium, paid for a real risk (left-tail variance shocks). Sellers earn the premium in normal regimes and pay back in stress. Sharpe is bounded; tails are real.
Not market-timing. We do not predict when vol spikes will occur. We size positions for capacity to absorb spikes and exit when current spreads breach pre-committed exit triggers.
Not idiosyncratic-stock-picking. The wheel basket is selected by liquidity and structural-criteria thresholds, not by subjective conviction. The 9 names are the universe, not picks.

title: Thesis: Why Variance Risk Premium
text:
The capacity-versus-edge tradeoff
Single-name short-vol structures generate higher per-trade premium but carry concentrated tail risk. Index-level structures generate smaller per-trade premium but diversify cross-name idiosyncratic risk.
Our cluster mixes both:

Indexes (SPX, RUT, NDX) for diversified equity-VRP capture
ETFs (TLT, GLD) for cross-asset diversification (bond and gold vol have low correlation with equity vol over multi-year windows)
Individual names (wheel basket) for incremental premium with sector spread

The expected payoff: combined book Sharpe higher than any single instrument, with maximum drawdown bounded by halt framework + per-instrument max-loss per spread.

title: Thesis: Why Variance Risk Premium
section: Why iron condor over single-side spread
text:
Why iron condor over single-side spread
The legacy strategy (v1.5 baseline) used put-credit spreads only. Adding the call wing converts to iron condor. Trade-offs:

Premium captured per structure: roughly doubles (both sides earn)
Defined risk per structure: wider per-structure max-loss (both wings can be in the money simultaneously, though rarely)
Trend exposure: put-side benefits from rising markets; call-side is hurt. Iron condor is delta-neutral at entry; one wing always offsets the other in trending regimes
Volatility exposure: symmetric, short vega on both sides. IV-crush after entry helps both wings

In strong trending markets (like 2018-2024 SPX), the call wing is structurally disadvantaged: spot rallies hard, calls go in the money, losses on calls partially offset gains on puts. Result: iron condor naked-mode Sharpe is below put-only naked-mode Sharpe in trending regimes (we observed exactly this in our diagnostic).
The strategy’s edge over naked-mode iron condor comes from the halt framework, exiting when market regime shifts to high-realized-vol environments where short-vol positions of any kind underperform.

title: Thesis: Why Variance Risk Premium
text:
Foundational pricing: Black-Scholes and Merton
Strike selection uses Black-Scholes Greeks: 16-delta short legs (one standard deviation OTM under the lognormal assumption), 5-point wings (or per-instrument-grid). The BS pricer is a fallback when OptionMetrics-published implied volatility is missing.
Black-Scholes empirically overvalues options on high-variance underlyings and undervalues low-variance, this is the published finding from BS’s own 1973 paper. That bias is itself the structural source of the volatility risk premium our strategy harvests. We do not “out-predict” the BS pricer; we systematically take the side of the trade where BS-implied premium exceeds realized variance over the holding window.
Merton’s 1973 extension covers American early-exercise (relevant for the wheel basket’s dividend-paying names) and continuous-dividend pricing. American puts on dividend-paying stocks always have positive probability of premature exercise (Merton Theorem 13). The wheel mechanic accepts assignment as a feature: when assigned shares, write covered calls until called away.

title: Results
text:
Sharpe ratios on this page are reported in two complementary forms:

Sharpe (excess), the headline. (annualized return − annualized risk-free) / annualized volatility.
Deflated Sharpe (DSR), corrects for selection bias when many baskets are tested. Uses an implied-independent-trials count rather than the raw trial count, since adjacent baskets share underlying-instrument exposure and inflate the apparent number of independent searches.

Other reported metrics:

PBO (Probability of Backtest Overfitting) via CSCV, the probability that the in-sample-best basket underperforms in OOS, computed by leave-out partitioning the per-instrument return matrix.
n_trades and win rate per instrument.
Max drawdown (signed, negative) and annualized return (geometric).

Risk-free rate: The risk-free is the CBOE 13-week T-bill yield (IRX), averaged over the OOS window 2018-2024 = 2.33% annualized. Excess Sharpe = (annualized return − 2.33%) / annualized volatility. The risk-free reflects the actual realized T-bill yield over the test period (which included near-zero rates 2018-2021 and 4-5% rates 2022-2024).
Acceptance gates locked in advance:

DSR (PSR threshold) ≥ 0.95 against the implied-independent-trials benchmark
PBO via CSCV ≤ 0.30 on the per-instrument return matrix
Reproducibility: same commit, same data, same seed → byte-identical equity curve

title: Reproducibility
text: Two runs of the same commit + the same data + the same SEED = 42 produce identical equity curves to floating-point precision. This page documents how to reproduce every number in the results page from a fresh checkout.

title: Reproducibility
text:
Environment

Python 3.12+ on Linux/macOS/WSL (tested on WSL Ubuntu 22.04)
~16 GB RAM (4–6 GB working set; SPX parquet is the largest single load at ~750 MB on disk)
~3 GB disk free for per-ticker parquets

title: Reproducibility

git clone <repo-url> FinTech533_capstone

python -m venv .venv

title: Reproducibility
text:
One-time data conversion
The OptionMetrics CSV (strat2.2.csv.gz, ~2.4 GB compressed, 68.4M rows) is converted to per-ticker parquets via DuckDB streaming. Without this step, loading the CSV via pandas exhausts WSL memory and crashes the session.
PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/convert_optionmetrics_to_parquet.py
Expected runtime: ~80 seconds. Output: 14 parquets in data/processed/options_by_ticker/{TICKER}.parquet, parity-checked against original CSV row counts. Idempotent (re-running with parquets in place is a no-op unless --force).

title: Reproducibility
text:
Reproduce headline results
# 1. Verify parquet conversion (52 parity tests)
PYTHONPATH=. pytest tests/test_optionmetrics_parquet_loader.py -v

# 2. Run all logic tests (no data load required)
PYTHONPATH=. pytest tests/ --ignore=tests/test_optionmetrics_parquet_loader.py -q
# Expected: 92/92 PASS

# 3. SPX halts_only diagnostic (sanity check on Layer 4 fix)
PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/diagnose_spx_halts_only.py
# Expected: Sharpe 0.497, 12 distinct halt periods, max 92 days

# 4. Multi-instrument NAKED runner (5 VRP tickers, ~10 min)
PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/run_multi_instrument_vrp.py --mode naked

# 5. Multi-instrument halts_only runner (5 VRP tickers, ~10 min)
PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/run_multi_instrument_vrp.py --mode halts_only

# 6. ML head training (Heads 1, 2, 3, Heads 1/3 reuse the multi-instrument output;
#    Head 2 is independent and uses features.parquet)
PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/run_head2_regime_stress.py
PYTHONPATH=. python scripts/train_head1_per_instrument.py

Data Sources
The strategy reads from three external data providers, all snapshotted to local parquet files at commit time. No live network connections occur during a backtest.

1. OptionMetrics IvyDB (option chains)
File: strat2.2.csv.gz (2.4 GB compressed, 68.4M rows) → split via scripts/convert_optionmetrics_to_parquet.py into per-ticker parquets at data/processed/options_by_ticker/{TICKER}.parquet.
Provides: daily option chains (date, exdate, cp_flag, strike, best_bid, best_offer, impl_volatility, delta, gamma, vega, theta, volume, open_interest) for 12 tickers spanning 2012-2025. Used by the engine to price entries and exits at real chain quotes (not BS-pricer fallback) wherever available.


2. WRDS OptionMetrics IvyDB Securities (per-ticker underlying OHLC)
File: wheelstrat_data.gz (querying WRDS via Duke subscription) → split via scripts/convert_wheelstrat_data.py into per-ticker parquets at data/raw/{TICKER}.parquet.
Provides: daily underlying OHLC (open, high, low, close, volume, return, cfadj) for the 4 headline-basket tickers (AAPL, MSFT, WMT, GLD) and 6 other instruments tested in the ablation matrix. Spans 2012-01-03 to 2025-08-29. Same secid system as the OptionMetrics chains, ensuring clean joins between underlying spot and option chains for the same security on the same date. Daily closes match published exchange records on spot-checked reference dates (e.g., AAPL 2018-04-16 = $175.82).


3. Interactive Brokers TWS feed snapshot (exogenous macro factors)
Files: data/raw/{VIX,VIX3M,VVIX,SKEW,IRX,TNX,HYG,LQD,SPY,SPX}.parquet. Snapshotted from the Interactive Brokers TWS market-data feed and frozen to local parquet at commit time. No live TWS connection is needed at backtest time.
Provides: macro / regime indicators (CBOE volatility indices, FRED Treasury yields, ETF macro tape, SPX bars for the market-wide gap-skip and Layer 1 hard halt). Spans 2011-05-05 to 2026-04-30 across the various series.

Determinism

SEED = 42 (in src/config.py) consumed by:

XGBoost random_state for every fit
sklearn IsotonicRegression (no randomness, but LogisticRegression for Platt: solver="lbfgs" is deterministic)

title: Live Monitoring Framework
text:
This is the answer to the two questions every trading-system writeup is supposed to address:
Both questions are answered with one framework: Hoeffding’s inequality, applied in the trader form.

title: Live Monitoring Framework
text:
The framework
Pre-commit a baseline performance metric μ from the OOS backtest, for our headline strategy, that’s the rolling-60-trade win rate observed over 2018–2024. Then, going forward, observe the live realized win rate X̄ over the same rolling-60-trade window. Apply:
\[
P[\,\bar X - \mu \geq t \mid H_0\,] \;\leq\; e^{-2 t^2 N}
\]
where t = μ − X̄ is the realized underperformance, N is the number of trades in the rolling window (60), and the bound is the maximum probability that the observed underperformance is due to chance alone, given the regime hypothesis H₀ (= “the OOS regime persists going forward”).
The bound is a distribution-free, worst-case probability. It holds for any bounded random variable regardless of the underlying distribution or autocorrelation structure. No assumptions about return distribution, no Newey-West, no Hodrick, just the inequality.

title: Live Monitoring Framework
text:
Threshold semantics (pre-committed)









Bound ≤ e^(−2t²N)
Signal
Interpretation
Action




≥ 50%
🟢 green
Observed underperformance plausibly chance
Continue normally


25–50%
🟡 yellow
Beliefs about regime probably no longer fully right
Consider stake reduction


10–25%
🟠 red
Significant regime risk
Substantial concern; review


< 10%
🔴 critical
Almost certain regime change
Halt strategy and rethink



These thresholds are pre-committed before live deployment. They are not numerical Sharpe targets, they are structural confidence-level cutoffs on the probability bound itself.

title: Live Monitoring Framework
text:
Why 60-trade rolling window
Three constraints determine the window size:

Statistical power. At N = 60 trades, an observed underperformance of t = 0.10 (10 percentage points below pre-committed win rate) gives a Hoeffding bound of e^(−2·0.01·60) = e^(−1.2) ≈ 30%. That puts a 10-point degradation in the yellow zone, which is the right level of sensitivity, not jumping at one bad week, not waiting for a year of declines.
Time-to-signal. With ~50–60 trades per year on the SPX iron condor at weekly cadence, 60 trades ≈ 1 year. The monitor produces a fresh signal monthly as the rolling window updates.
Distribution stability. Hoeffding holds for any bounded RV, but tighter bands of t for the same N require either more trades or larger underperformance magnitude. 60 is the smallest N at which the threshold-semantics resolution is meaningful for win-rate observations bounded in [0, 1].

Notable: the headline basket’s rolling win rate at the COVID crash check-date (60-trade window ending Jan 2020) was 85%, actually above the pre-committed μ. The defined-risk put-credit-spread structure with halt framework absorbed the COVID stress without measurable win-rate degradation in the rolling window. The framework demonstrates three properties on this retrospective:

Not noise-driven, 88% of windows stay green, indicating low false-positive rate from random monthly fluctuations.
Sensitive enough to flag genuine dips, 4.2% of windows reach the red zone (10-25% bound), meaning the framework would have alerted human attention at those moments.
No catastrophic firing, 0% critical signals over 7 years means the strategy did not experience a regime-degradation event large enough to trigger a forced shutdown. Validation that the basket is robust within its pre-committed expectations.

title: Live Monitoring Framework
section: What the framework does NOT do
text:
What the framework does NOT do

It does not predict that a regime change is about to happen. It detects degradation that has already occurred.
It does not distinguish between bad luck on a small sample and a true regime change. The bound is a probability statement, not a binary decision. Reading the bound at 30% means “this could be bad luck, possible, but it could also be regime degradation; the monitor flags it for human attention.”
It does not adapt μ over time. We commit μ from the OOS backtest and hold it. If we update μ live, we lose the pre-commitment property and the framework becomes circular.

title: Live Monitoring Framework
text:
Implementation
The monitor is implemented in src/metrics/hoeffding.py and scripts/hoeffding_monitor.py. It reads per-instrument trade outcomes, computes the rolling-60 win rate, applies the bound, and emits a dated alert log to data/processed/hoeffding_signals/{TICKER}_signals.parquet.
Cadence in production: weekly run, one signal per Monday morning before any new entries fire. Output: per-instrument signal status + book-level signal aggregated across the 5 VRP and 9 wheel positions.

title: Live Monitoring Framework
text:
What this answers
For the question “how will you know if the strategy is performing as expected?”, the bound stays ≥ 50% (green). Performance is plausibly within the OOS regime.
For the question “how will you quantify when it stops working?”, when the bound drops to 10% or below, the strategy has degraded enough that random chance is an implausible explanation. That is the trip-wire. It is dated, quantitative, distribution-free, and pre-committed.
